claim: FOXO transcription factors are critical regulators of cell homeostasis and steer cell death, differentiation and longevity in mammalian cells.
source: FOXO transcription factors are critical regulators of cell homeostasis and steer cell death, differentiation and longevity in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about FOXO function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Compound S9 and its oxalate salt S9OX physically interact with the DNA-binding domain (DBD) of FOXO3.
source: We demonstrate that compounds S9 and its oxalate salt S9OX interfere with FOXO3 target promoter binding, gene transcription and modulate the physiologic program activated by FOXO3 in cancer cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents NMR spectroscopy data (Figure 2) and FPA data (Figure 1f) demonstrating direct physical interaction between S9/S9OX and FOXO3-DBD.

claim: S9 and S9OX interfere with FOXO3 target promoter binding.
source: We demonstrate that compounds S9 and its oxalate salt S9OX interfere with FOXO3 target promoter binding, gene transcription and modulate the physiologic program activated by FOXO3 in cancer cells.
evidence: ChIP analyses in Figure 4e demonstrate reduced FOXO3 binding to target promoters in the presence of S9.

claim: S9 and S9OX modulate FOXO3 gene transcription.
source: We demonstrate that compounds S9 and its oxalate salt S9OX interfere with FOXO3 target promoter binding, gene transcription and modulate the physiologic program activated by FOXO3 in cancer cells.
evidence: Microarray data (Figure 3) and qRT-PCR data (Figure 3d-g) show that S9/S9OX affect FOXO3-mediated gene expression.

claim: The FOXO-DBD is druggable.
source: These small molecules prove the druggability of the FOXO-DBD and provide a structural basis for modulating these important homeostasis regulators in normal and malignant cells.
evidence: The identification of S9 as a small molecule that binds to FOXO3-DBD and modulates its function provides experimental evidence for druggability.

claim: Mammalian FOXO family members recognize and bind the same core DNA elements (TTGTTTAC).
source: In mammals, FOXO3 and its family members recognize and bind the same core DNA elements (TTGTTTAC) to control the transcription of direct target genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FOXO DNA binding consensus sequences.

claim: FOXO3 was initially considered as a tumor suppressor that induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.
source: FOXO3 was initially considered as a tumor suppressor that induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest (Calnan and Brunet, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXO3 has functions in cellular detoxification.
source: However, its functions in cellular detoxification (de Keizer et al., 2011; Salcher et al., 2014), and drug-resistance (Hui et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2011), maintenance of cancer stem cells (Naka et al., 2010) as well as inhibition of other death-inducers such as TP53 (Rupp et al., 2017) suggest also a tumor-promoting role in certain types of cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXO3 has functions in drug-resistance.
source: However, its functions in cellular detoxification (de Keizer et al., 2011; Salcher et al., 2014), and drug-resistance (Hui et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2011), maintenance of cancer stem cells (Naka et al., 2010) as well as inhibition of other death-inducers such as TP53 (Rupp et al., 2017) suggest also a tumor-promoting role in certain types of cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXO3 has functions in maintenance of cancer stem cells.
source: However, its functions in cellular detoxification (de Keizer et al., 2011; Salcher et al., 2014), and drug-resistance (Hui et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2011), maintenance of cancer stem cells (Naka et al., 2010) as well as inhibition of other death-inducers such as TP53 (Rupp et al., 2017) suggest also a tumor-promoting role in certain types of cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXO3 inhibits other death-inducers such as TP53.
source: However, its functions in cellular detoxification (de Keizer et al., 2011; Salcher et al., 2014), and drug-resistance (Hui et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2011), maintenance of cancer stem cells (Naka et al., 2010) as well as inhibition of other death-inducers such as TP53 (Rupp et al., 2017) suggest also a tumor-promoting role in certain types of cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXO3 has a tumor-promoting role in certain types of cancer.
source: However, its functions in cellular detoxification (de Keizer et al., 2011; Salcher et al., 2014), and drug-resistance (Hui et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2011), maintenance of cancer stem cells (Naka et al., 2010) as well as inhibition of other death-inducers such as TP53 (Rupp et al., 2017) suggest also a tumor-promoting role in certain types of cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited functions of FOXO3 in drug resistance, cancer stem cell maintenance, and inhibition of death inducers.

claim: The pro-proliferative PI3K-PKB pathway inactivates FOXO3 target gene transcription.
source: Multiple cellular signaling pathways converge on FOXO3, most importantly the pro-proliferative PI3K-PKB pathway that inactivates target gene transcription.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FOXO3 regulation.

claim: Stress conditions override growth-factor-mediated phosphorylation of FOXO3, resulting in relocation of FOXO3 to the nucleus.
source: On the other hand, stress conditions, such as genotoxic stress, reactive oxygen species (ROS) or hypoxic stress, override growth-factor-mediated phosphorylation of FOXO3, which results in the relocation of FOXO3 to the nucleus (Hagenbuchner et al., 2012; Hagenbuchner et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Stress induced signaling kinases such as JNK or MST1 cause FOXO3 activation and nuclear accumulation in presence of PKB signaling.
source: Thereby, stress induced signaling kinases, such as JNK or MST1 that cause FOXO3 activation and nuclear accumulation also in presence of PKB signaling critically contribute to FOXO3-triggered therapy-resistance programs that protect cancer cells during therapy (Hagenbuchner et al., 2016b; Rupp et al., 2017; Naka et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXO3 regulates the differentiation of naïve regulatory T-cells via its transcriptional target FOXP3.
source: In addition, FOXO3 regulates the differentiation of naïve regulatory T-cells via its transcriptional target FOXP3 (Kerdiles et al., 2010; Harada et al., 2010), which limits the cytotoxic anti-cancer T-cell response by immune-suppressive regulatory T-cells that infiltrate tumor tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FOXP3 limits the cytotoxic anti-cancer T-cell response by immune-suppressive regulatory T-cells that infiltrate tumor tissue.
source: In addition, FOXO3 regulates the differentiation of naïve regulatory T-cells via its transcriptional target FOXP3 (Kerdiles et al., 2010; Harada et al., 2010), which limits the cytotoxic anti-cancer T-cell response by immune-suppressive regulatory T-cells that infiltrate tumor tissue.
evidence: This is established knowledge about regulatory T-cell function in cancer.

claim: Reversible inhibition of FOXO3 activity by small compounds might boost anti-tumor immune responses.
source: A reversible inhibition of FOXO3 activity by small compounds thereby might boost anti-tumor immune responses and limit side effects of FOXO3 functional inactivation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The DNA binding domain (DBD) of transcription factors are usually regarded as 'undruggable' due to large surfaces and the fact that the only known ligand is a DNA molecule.
source: In contrast to the small, defined substrate binding pockets on catalytic enzymes, the DNA binding domain (DBD) of transcription factors are usually regarded as 'undruggable' due to the large surfaces and the fact that the only known ligand is a DNA molecule.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge in the field of drug discovery.

claim: Small molecules have been described for the transcription factor FOXM1.
source: Small molecules have been described for the transcription factor FOXM1 (Gormally et al., 2014; Hegde et al., 2011) and one compound was shown to regulate FOXO1 activity (Nagashima et al., 2010), but no compounds have been discovered that directly physically interact with the DBD of FOXO proteins to regulate their transcriptional activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One compound was shown to regulate FOXO1 activity.
source: Small molecules have been described for the transcription factor FOXM1 (Gormally et al., 2014; Hegde et al., 2011) and one compound was shown to regulate FOXO1 activity (Nagashima et al., 2010), but no compounds have been discovered that directly physically interact with the DBD of FOXO proteins to regulate their transcriptional activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No compounds have been discovered that directly physically interact with the DBD of FOXO proteins to regulate their transcriptional activity prior to this study.
source: Small molecules have been described for the transcription factor FOXM1 (Gormally et al., 2014; Hegde et al., 2011) and one compound was shown to regulate FOXO1 activity (Nagashima et al., 2010), but no compounds have been discovered that directly physically interact with the DBD of FOXO proteins to regulate their transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: S9 inhibits FOXO3-binding to target promoters.
source: By a pharmacophore model-based, virtual in silico screening approach we identified compound S9 and demonstrate that this molecule inhibits FOXO3-binding to target promoters, affects the cell-wide transcriptional program of FOXO3, as well as FOXO3 effects on cellular ROS-production and cell growth in 2D and 3D cell culture systems.
evidence: ChIP data in Figure 4e demonstrates this effect.

claim: S9 affects the cell-wide transcriptional program of FOXO3.
source: By a pharmacophore model-based, virtual in silico screening approach we identified compound S9 and demonstrate that this molecule inhibits FOXO3-binding to target promoters, affects the cell-wide transcriptional program of FOXO3, as well as FOXO3 effects on cellular ROS-production and cell growth in 2D and 3D cell culture systems.
evidence: Microarray data in Figure 3 demonstrates genome-wide transcriptional changes.

claim: S9 affects FOXO3 effects on cellular ROS-production.
source: By a pharmacophore model-based, virtual in silico screening approach we identified compound S9 and demonstrate that this molecule inhibits FOXO3-binding to target promoters, affects the cell-wide transcriptional program of FOXO3, as well as FOXO3 effects on cellular ROS-production and cell growth in 2D and 3D cell culture systems.
evidence: ROS measurements in Figure 6a-b demonstrate this effect.

claim: S9 affects FOXO3 effects on cell growth in 2D and 3D cell culture systems.
source: By a pharmacophore model-based, virtual in silico screening approach we identified compound S9 and demonstrate that this molecule inhibits FOXO3-binding to target promoters, affects the cell-wide transcriptional program of FOXO3, as well as FOXO3 effects on cellular ROS-production and cell growth in 2D and 3D cell culture systems.
evidence: Cell death data in Figure 1g and 3D spheroid data in Figure 6c-g demonstrate these effects.

claim: S9 directly interacts with FOXO3 DBD as demonstrated by NMR.
source: By NMR we demonstrate that S9 directly interacts with FOXO3 DBD, elucidate the mode of binding and how this molecule structurally interferes with FOXO3 transcriptional activity.
evidence: NMR data in Figure 2 demonstrates direct binding.

claim: A structure-based modeling workflow was developed employing the crystal structure of FOXO3 DBD in complex with a 13 bp FOXO3 consensus sequence DNA strand (PDB entry 2UZK).
source: In the absence of known small molecule ligands, a structure-based modeling workflow (Figure 1a) was developed, employing the crystal structure of FOXO3 DBD in complex with a 13 bp FOXO3 consensus sequence DNA strand (PDB entry 2UZK; Tsai et al., 2007).
evidence: The workflow is described in the text and shown in Figure 1a, using a published crystal structure.

claim: Six pharmacophore models were generated for virtual screening.
source: The identified binding patterns were represented by six pharmacophore models, which were subsequently used for virtual screening of the Specs (www.specs.net) and Maybridge (www.maybridge.com) databases.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used.

claim: 76 virtual hits were selected for experimental testing.
source: 76 virtual hits for which the desired binding mode was confirmed by further docking studies were selected for experimental testing.
evidence: This describes the number of compounds selected from virtual screening.

claim: Compound S9 (1-(4,6-dimethylpyrimidin-2-yl)−3-(4-propoxyphenyl)guanidine) was identified by pharmacophore model 1.
source: Compound S9 (1-(4,6-dimethylpyrimidin-2-yl)−3-(4-propoxyphenyl)guanidine) was identified by pharmacophore model 1 (Figure 1e).
evidence: The identification of S9 is stated in text and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: S9 dose-dependently increases freely rotating oligonucleotide in FPA with recombinant FOXO3-DBD.
source: FPA of recombinant FOXO3-DBD (125 nM) and FAM-labeled IRE-oligonucleotide (25 nM). S9 dose-dependent increase of freely rotating oligonucleotide is demonstrated.
evidence: Figure 1f shows dose-dependent FPA data.

claim: S9 and S9OX inhibit FOXO3-induced cell death in SH-EP/FOXO3 cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 1g (and Figure 1—figure supplement 1bc), the addition of compound S9 and S9OX interfered with FOXO3-induced cell death in a dose-dependent manner to similar extent, demonstrating that S9 and the oxalate salt S9OX enter living cells and modulate FOXO3 function.
evidence: Figure 1g shows dose-dependent cell death inhibition data.

claim: S9 and S9OX enter living cells.
source: As shown in Figure 1g (and Figure 1—figure supplement 1bc), the addition of compound S9 and S9OX interfered with FOXO3-induced cell death in a dose-dependent manner to similar extent, demonstrating that S9 and the oxalate salt S9OX enter living cells and modulate FOXO3 function.
evidence: The ability to modulate FOXO3 function in cell-based assays implies cell permeability.

claim: STD signals were detected for several protons of both S9 and its oxalate salt in NMR measurements with FOXO3-DBD.
source: STD signals were detected for several protons of both S9 and its oxalate salt, thus confirming their interaction with FOXO3-DBD (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a show STD NMR data.

claim: Both aromatic moieties as well as the aliphatic part of S9 are involved in direct interactions with FOXO3-DBD.
source: These data suggested that both aromatic moieties as well as the aliphatic part of S9 are involved in direct interactions with FOXO3-DBD.
evidence: This is inferred from the STD NMR signal patterns observed for different protons of S9.

claim: Thirteen residues of FOXO3-DBD whose 1H-15N resonances were significantly perturbed (1σ0corr above the mean) upon S9OX binding.
source: The presence of S9OX induced significant dose-dependent CSPs of backbone amide groups of fifteen FOXO3-DBD residues (the chemical shift change was greater than σ0corr above the mean), thus suggesting their involvement in the interaction or their conformational change induced by S9 binding (Figure 2b).
evidence: Figure 2b shows CSP data identifying affected residues.

claim: The most affected residues by S9OX binding were Arg211, His212, Asn213, Ser215 and Leu216 from helix H3; Phe220 and Asn237 from wing W2; and Thr167 from helix H1.
source: The most affected residues (the chemical shift change was greater than 2σ0corr above the mean) were Arg211, His212, Asn213, Ser215 and Leu216 from the helix H3; Phe220 and Asn237 from the wing W2; and Thr167 from the helix H1.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of CSP data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: S9OX binding to FOXO3-DBD is of moderate affinity based on fast exchange on the NMR time scale.
source: In addition, the gradual shift of resonances during titration indicated fast exchange of the ligand on the NMR time scale, thus suggesting that the S9OX binding is of moderate affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR titration behavior observed in the experiments.

claim: S9 binds into the groove formed by residues Arg211, His212 and Ser215 at the C-terminus of α-helix H3 and residues Met221 and Arg222 from the N-terminus of β-strand S2.
source: The final pose is consistent with results from both STD and 1H-15N HSQC experiments and suggests that S9 binds into the groove formed by residues Arg211, His212 and Ser215 at the C-terminus of α-helix H3 and residues Met221 and Arg222 from the N-terminus of β-strand S2.
evidence: This is based on molecular docking calculations validated against NMR data.

claim: The DNA recognition α-helix H3 is responsible for most of the direct base contacts with DNA.
source: This region is a crucial part of the FOXO3-DBD/DNA interface as the DNA recognition α-helix H3 is responsible for most of the direct base contacts with DNA and the N-terminal part of β-strand S2 is involved in contacts with the DNA backbone (Tsai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural studies.

claim: The N-terminal part of β-strand S2 is involved in contacts with the DNA backbone.
source: This region is a crucial part of the FOXO3-DBD/DNA interface as the DNA recognition α-helix H3 is responsible for most of the direct base contacts with DNA and the N-terminal part of β-strand S2 is involved in contacts with the DNA backbone (Tsai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural studies.

claim: S9 binding blocks the DNA binding surface of FOXO3-DBD in the region of the recognition α-helix H3.
source: Therefore, these data indicate that S9 binding blocks the DNA binding surface of FOXO3-DBD in the region of the recognition α-helix H3.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding site location determined by NMR and docking studies.

claim: 1262 probesets were induced upon activation of ectopic FOXO3(A3)ERtm in SH-EP/FOXO3 cells treated with 50 nM 4OHT for three hours.
source: 1262 probesets were induced and 889 probesets showed statistically significant repression upon activation of ectopic FOXO3(A3)ERtm as demonstrated in heatmaps (Figure 3a) and volcano blots (Figure 3b).
evidence: Microarray data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: 889 probesets showed statistically significant repression upon activation of ectopic FOXO3(A3)ERtm.
source: 1262 probesets were induced and 889 probesets showed statistically significant repression upon activation of ectopic FOXO3(A3)ERtm as demonstrated in heatmaps (Figure 3a) and volcano blots (Figure 3b).
evidence: Microarray data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: When 4OHT-driven activation of ectopic FOXO3 was combined with S9, only 208 probesets were upregulated.
source: When 4OHT-driven activation of ectopic FOXO3 was combined with S9, the gene induction was much less pronounced, with the expression of only 208 probesets upregulated of which 35 were common with FOXO3 activation alone (Figure 3c).
evidence: Microarray data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: 35 probesets were commonly upregulated by FOXO3 activation alone and FOXO3 activation with S9.
source: When 4OHT-driven activation of ectopic FOXO3 was combined with S9, the gene induction was much less pronounced, with the expression of only 208 probesets upregulated of which 35 were common with FOXO3 activation alone (Figure 3c).
evidence: Venn diagram in Figure 3c shows overlap.

claim: 193 probesets showed significant repression in presence of S9, suggesting inhibition of FOXO3-mediated induction.
source: We examined whether the presence of S9 reversed FOXO3-mediated gene induction and identified 193 probesets showing significant repression in presence of S9, suggesting an inhibition of FOXO3-mediated induction (Figure 3b).
evidence: Microarray data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: S9 inhibited FOXO3-mediated induction of 77% of FOXO3 induced probesets overall (15% statistically significant).
source: Furthermore, 779 probesets have shown the reversal of expression although they did not reach statistical significance. This suggests that S9 inhibited FOXO3-mediated induction of the majority of mRNAs (77% of FOXO3 induced probesets overall, 15% statistically significant).
evidence: This is calculated from the microarray data analysis.

claim: Activation of ectopically-expressed FOXO3(A3)ERtm by 4OHT significantly induced steady state expression of BIM, NOXA, SESN3 and DEPP1.
source: As shown in Figure 3d–g, activation of ectopically-expressed FOXO3(A3)ERtm by 4OHT significantly induced steady state expression of the pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins BIM and NOXA, as well as of the detoxifying proteins SESN3 and DEPP1 similar to previously published data from our group (Hagenbuchner et al., 2012; Obexer et al., 2007; Salcher et al., 2014; Salcher et al., 2017).
evidence: qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3d-g.

claim: S9 or S9OX alone caused no statistically significant changes in steady state expression of BIM, NOXA, SESN3 and DEPP1 compared to solvent-treated controls.
source: S9 or S9OX alone caused no statistically significant changes in steady state expression of these genes compared to solvent-treated controls.
evidence: This is stated based on qRT-PCR data in Figure 3d-g.

claim: When combined with activation of ectopic FOXO3, S9 and S9OX significantly counteracted mRNA induction of BIM, NOXA, SESN3 and DEPP1.
source: However, when combined with activation of ectopic FOXO3, S9 as well S9OX significantly counteracted mRNA induction of all four bona fide FOXO3 targets suggesting that this compound efficiently interferes with specific mRNA induction by FOXO3.
evidence: qRT-PCR data in Figure 3d-g demonstrates this effect.

claim: Activation of the 4OHT-regulated FOXO3(A3)ERtm transgene elevated protein levels of BIM, NOXA, SESN3 and DEPP1.
source: As shown in Figure 4a–d the activation of the 4OHT-regulated FOXO3(A3)ERtm transgene in SH-EP/FOXO3 neuroblastoma cells elevated the protein levels of the proteins BIM, NOXA, SESN3 and DEPP1.
evidence: Immunoblot data shown in Figure 4a-d.

claim: Both S9 and S9OX prevented FOXO3-mediated induction of NOXA, BIM and SESN3 above background level.
source: Consistent with quantitative RT-PCR results in Figure 3d–g, both S9 and S9OX prevented FOXO3-mediated induction of NOXA, BIM and SESN3 above background level and significantly attenuated the strong induction of DEPP1, demonstrating that S9 and S9OX efficiently interfere with the regulation of FOXO3 target proteins in living cells.
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 4a-d demonstrates this effect.

claim: S9 and S9OX significantly attenuated the strong induction of DEPP1 by FOXO3.
source: Consistent with quantitative RT-PCR results in Figure 3d–g, both S9 and S9OX prevented FOXO3-mediated induction of NOXA, BIM and SESN3 above background level and significantly attenuated the strong induction of DEPP1, demonstrating that S9 and S9OX efficiently interfere with the regulation of FOXO3 target proteins in living cells.
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 4a-d demonstrates this effect.

claim: Activation of the conditional FOXO3 allele for three hours significantly increased FOXO3 promoter binding to BIM, NOXA, SESN3 and DEPP1 promoters.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 4e, activation of the conditional FOXO3 allele for three hours significantly increased FOXO3 promoter binding, which is consistent with the previously demonstrated induction of these FOXO3 targets on mRNA and protein level.
evidence: ChIP data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The addition of S9 almost completely reduced the interaction of FOXO3 with endogenous BIM, NOXA, SESN3 and DEPP1 promoters to control level.
source: Importantly, for all investigated promoters, the addition of S9 almost completely reduced the interaction of FOXO3 with endogenous promoters to control level.
evidence: ChIP data in Figure 4e demonstrates this effect.

claim: Compound S9 reduced luciferase activity driven by a 544 bp DEPP1 promoter fragment in a dose-dependent manner with approximately 50% reduction at 12.5 µM.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 4f, compound S9 reduced luciferase activity in a dose-dependent manner with approximately 50% reduction at 12.5 µM.
evidence: Luciferase reporter data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Activation of FOXO3(A3)-H212R still induced apoptotic cell death in SH-EP cells although to a significantly lower extent than the FOXO3(A3) construct.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 5a activation of FOXO3(A3)-H212R still induced apoptotic cell death in SH-EP cells although to a significantly lower extent than the FOXO3(A3) construct.
evidence: Cell death data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: S9 did not affect apoptosis induced by the FOXO3(A3)-H212R mutant.
source: However, in contrast to FOXO3(A3)-induced cell death, S9 did not affect apoptosis by the FOXO3(A3)-H212R mutant suggesting that the H212 mutation completely abrogates FOXO3-inhibitory effects of S9.
evidence: Cell death data in Figure 5a demonstrates this lack of effect.

claim: The H212 mutation completely abrogates FOXO3-inhibitory effects of S9.
source: However, in contrast to FOXO3(A3)-induced cell death, S9 did not affect apoptosis by the FOXO3(A3)-H212R mutant suggesting that the H212 mutation completely abrogates FOXO3-inhibitory effects of S9.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of S9 effect on the H212R mutant shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Etoposide treatment increases promoter activity of the BIM and DEPP1 promoters two- to threefold in cells with endogenous FOXO3.
source: As shown in Figure 5bc, etoposide treatment increases promoter activity of the BIM and the DEPP1 promoter two- to threefold and S9 completely prevents this induction.
evidence: Luciferase reporter data shown in Figure 5b-c.

claim: S9 completely prevents etoposide-induced increase in BIM and DEPP1 promoter activity.
source: As shown in Figure 5bc, etoposide treatment increases promoter activity of the BIM and the DEPP1 promoter two- to threefold and S9 completely prevents this induction.
evidence: Luciferase reporter data shown in Figure 5b-c.

claim: Knockout of endogenous FOXO3 abrogates the effect of etoposide treatment on FOXO3-responsive promoters.
source: Knockout of endogenous FOXO3 abrogates the effect of etoposide treatment on FOXO3-responsive promoters and S9 does not further affect promoter activity suggesting that the inhibitory effect of S9 depends on the presence of endogenous FOXO3 protein and is not due to unspecific effects on transcription.
evidence: Luciferase reporter data in Figure 5b-c with FOXO3 knockout cells.

claim: The inhibitory effect of S9 depends on the presence of endogenous FOXO3 protein.
source: Knockout of endogenous FOXO3 abrogates the effect of etoposide treatment on FOXO3-responsive promoters and S9 does not further affect promoter activity suggesting that the inhibitory effect of S9 depends on the presence of endogenous FOXO3 protein and is not due to unspecific effects on transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of S9 effect in FOXO3 knockout cells shown in Figure 5b-f.

claim: At a concentration of 250 nM, S9 most efficiently displaced the FAM-labelled IRE-oligonucleotide from FOXO3-DBD and FOXO4-DBD.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, at a concentration of 250 nM, S9 most efficiently displaced the FAM-labelled IRE-oligonucleotide from FOXO3-DBD and FOXO4-DBD and had a less pronounced effect on FOXO1-DBD.
evidence: FPA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: S9 had a less pronounced effect on FOXO1-DBD compared to FOXO3-DBD and FOXO4-DBD.
source: As demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, at a concentration of 250 nM, S9 most efficiently displaced the FAM-labelled IRE-oligonucleotide from FOXO3-DBD and FOXO4-DBD and had a less pronounced effect on FOXO1-DBD.
evidence: FPA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: S9 did not interfere with FOXO6-DBD – DNA binding.
source: Interestingly, the substance did not interfere with FOXO6-DBD – DNA binding at all.
evidence: FPA data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a shows no effect on FOXO6.

claim: The amino acid sequences of FOXO-DBDs are highly homologous, but NMR solution structures reveal significant differences between the DBDs of these closely related proteins.
source: Differential binding/selectivity for FOXO-family members might be explained by the fact that although the amino acid sequences of FOXO-DBDs are highly homologous, NMR solution structures reveal significant differences between the DBDs of these closely related proteins (Psenakova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: S9 did not affect FOXM1-DBD – DNA interaction at 500 nM.
source: To assess whether S9 might exert effects by binding to other important forkhead proteins such as FOXM1 we also established an FP-assay for the FOXM1-DBD, analyzed S9 effects at 500 nM and observed no effect on FOXM1-DBD – DNA interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: FPA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: NMR spectroscopy measurements demonstrated differential effects of S9OX on 1H and 15N chemical shift perturbations of backbone amide groups in 15N-labeled FOXO1-DBD, FOXO3-DBD and FOXO4-DBD proteins.
source: To further complement these analyses with direct binding studies we performed NMR spectroscopy measurements which demonstrated differential effects of S9OX on 1H and 15N chemical shift perturbations of backbone amide groups in 15N-labeled FOXO1-DBD, FOXO3-DBD and FOXO4-DBD proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Direct activation of ectopic FOXO3 by 4OHT causes significant accumulation of cellular ROS.
source: Direct activation of ectopic FOXO3 by 4OHT or etoposide treatment cause significant accumulation of cellular ROS as demonstrated by live-cell fluorescence microscopy using the ROS-sensitive dye reduced mitotracker red.
evidence: ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Etoposide treatment causes significant accumulation of cellular ROS.
source: Direct activation of ectopic FOXO3 by 4OHT or etoposide treatment cause significant accumulation of cellular ROS as demonstrated by live-cell fluorescence microscopy using the ROS-sensitive dye reduced mitotracker red.
evidence: ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Both S9 and S9OX completely prevent ROS accumulation in 4OHT- and etoposide-treated cells.
source: Both S9 and S9OX completely prevent ROS accumulation in 4OHT- and etoposide-treated cells demonstrating that S9 and S9OX efficiently prevent cellular ROS accumulation in response to FOXO3 activation.
evidence: ROS measurement data shown in Figure 6a-b.

claim: Both S9 and S9OX prevented FOXO3-induced cell death in 3D tumor spheroids at a concentration of 5 µM after single administration.
source: Both, S9 and S9OX prevented FOXO3-induced cell death in 3D tumor spheroids at a concentration of 5 µM and after single administration.
evidence: 3D spheroid data shown in Figure 6c-g.

claim: S9 and S9OX preserved the viability of tumor spheres and strongly inhibited the apoptosis-inducing effect of FOXO3 in 3D tumor model.
source: Importantly, ATP-content and resazurin salt reduction, which are both parameters for cell viability, demonstrated that S9 and S9OX preserved the viability of tumor spheres and strongly inhibited the apoptosis-inducing effect of FOXO3 in this 3D tumor model.
evidence: ATP and resazurin reduction data shown in Figure 6f-g.

claim: S9 and its oxalate salt S9OX physically interact with the FOXO3-DBD in the low micromolar range in living cells.
source: The combined data demonstrate that S9 and its oxalate salt S9OX physically interact with the FOXO3-DBD, inhibit FOXO3 transcriptional program and modulate FOXO3 physiologic function in the low micromolar range in living cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple experimental results from FPA, NMR, cell-based assays, and 3D spheroid experiments.

claim: FOXO3 activation induces a bi-phasic reactive oxygen species (ROS) wave that critically contributes to induction of apoptotic cell death in human neuroblastoma cells.
source: We previously demonstrated that FOXO3-activation induces a bi-phasic reactive oxygen species (ROS) wave that critically contributes to induction of apoptotic cell death in human neuroblastoma cells (Hagenbuchner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The FPA assay for FOXO3-DBD has a Z´factor of 0.6499.
source: The analysis provided a Z ́factor of 0.6499 which proves that the FPA is reliable for high-throughput screening (Z ́> 0.5).
evidence: Z´factor calculation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d.

claim: A Z´factor > 0.5 proves that an assay is reliable for high-throughput screening.
source: The analysis provided a Z ́factor of 0.6499 which proves that the FPA is reliable for high-throughput screening (Z ́> 0.5).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of assay development.

claim: S9 might sterically hamper protein-protein interactions that take place at the FOXO3-DBD such as the binding of the tumor suppressor protein TP53.
source: Of note S9 might also sterically hamper protein-protein interactions that take place at the FOXO3-DBD such as the binding of the tumor suppressor protein TP53 (Rupp et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the binding location of S9 and known protein-protein interactions at the FOXO3-DBD.

claim: Gene-dosage effects of FOXO3 lead to, in part, contrary physiological outcomes.
source: Interestingly, the growth-inhibitory effects of FOXO3 were only partially inhibited, which corresponds to the observation that gene-dosage effects of FOXO3 lead to, in part, contrary physiological outcomes (Hagenbuchner et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of FOXO3 exerts anti-cancer effects in cancer immunity.
source: FOXO transcription factors have been implicated in a plethora of different cellular functions, in cancer immunity where loss of FOXO3 exerts anti-cancer effects, but also hampers other arms of the immune system (Luo and Li, 2018), in neuronal development and plasticity (McLaughlin and Broihier, 2018), cancer angiogenesis and metabolism (Yadav et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The permanent ablation of FOXO activity in mammals is excluded as a therapeutic option due to the plethora of FOXO functions.
source: This excludes the permanent ablation of FOXO activity in mammals as a therapeutic option.
evidence: This is inferred from the diverse and important functions of FOXO proteins described in the preceding sentence.

claim: The DBD of FOXO transcription factors participates in intra- and intermolecular interactions with other cellular key regulators of death and longevity, such as TP53.
source: More complexity is added by the fact that the DBD of FOXO transcription factors participates in intra-, but also intermolecular interactions with other cellular key regulators of death and longevity, such as TP53 (Wang et al., 2008) and thereby also affects drug resistance (Rupp et al., 2017; Salcher et al., 2019) or aging (Baar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Due to its mode of binding, S9 might interfere with protein-protein interactions at the FOXO3-DBD.
source: Due to its mode of binding, S9 might well interfere with some of these protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is speculative based on the binding site of S9 overlapping with known protein-protein interaction sites.

claim: Small drug-like molecules such as S9 allow strict control of application-dose and -time.
source: The advantage of small drug-like molecules such as S9 is the strict control of application-dose and -time and the fact that they are not immunogenic allowing repeated applications – so dose- and application time can be adjusted to damage cancer cells or boost anti-cancer immunity, but also limit unwanted side effects of FOXO-inhibition on stem cells and other somatic tissues.
evidence: This is general knowledge about advantages of small molecule drugs.
